newsitem.title: UK: International Antarctic expedition gets under way.
newsitem.headline: International Antarctic expedition gets under way.

text.p: A unique expedition to the Antarctic gets under way on Wednesday, bringing together young people from countries in conflict in a bid to foster mutual trust and environmental awareness.
The 35-strong team from 26 countries include a Palestinian and an Israeli, a Catholic and Protestant from Northern Ireland, and a black and white South African.
Others among the group of 16-24 year olds, sponsored by the United Nations cultural organisation UNESCO, have overcome problems with drugs or alcohol.

"The purpose is to get these particularly interesting conflict couples working together as a team and to get them understanding group dynamics and the importance of survival on the ice, which depends on trusting other people," said expedition spokesman Robin Dunseath.
"These people will go into the Antarctic and will be so completely overawed by what they find there that they will then return home and will be made special envoys for UNESCO.
"They will be charged with taking the message home and speaking to clubs, schools and universities about the Antarctic," Dunseath told Reuters.

The first group of 17 youngsters leave Britain on Wednesday for Argentina where the full team will assemble for leadership training from a former member of Britain's elite SAS (Special Air Services) crack troops.

"Five days later they will understand what it means to be a member of a team. They will understand what it is, for example, to put your life in the hands of a Catholic if you are a Protestant," Dunseath said.
They will then board a Russian icebreaking ship for a month-long voyage around the Antarctic.

The explorers were selected for the privately-funded Tandem One Step Beyond Challenge with the help of government and voluntary organisations, for their backgrounds, potential and enthusiasm. The only condition was that they all speak English.

The plan is that they will be joined on the ship by British explorer Robert Swan, who is currently on an 800-mile trek from the South Pole to the edge of Antarctica to mark the 50th anniversary of UNESCO.

Swan has already walked the other 900 miles (1,450 km) of Antarctica in a 1986 expedition tracing the footsteps of the early 20th century British explorer Captain Robert Scott and hopes to cross the continent on foot.

The young people taking part in the expedition come from Argentina, Chile, Bosnia, Brazil, Mexico, Chechnya, Russia, Hong Kong, China, France, Greenland, Netherlands, Israel, the self-rule Palestinian Authority, India, Pakistan, Northern Ireland, Romania, Scotland, South Africa, Sweden, the United Arab Emirates, Tanzania, England, the United States and Vietnam.
